source.title: Safety Alignment Backfires: Preventing the Re-emergence of Suppressed Concepts in Fine-tuned Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
source.authors: Sanghyun Kim; Moonseok Choi; Jinwoo Shin; Juho Lee

record.tranche_reason: Extends the safety-fine-tuning question to safety-aligned text-to-image diffusion models and reports results, but does not test the chat refusal or token-position behaviours named in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The study tests whether fine-tuning safety-aligned diffusion models brings back unsafe image content. Those image-generation outcomes are not chat-model refusals or compliance with a user's harmful request, so they are recorded as related findings under fits_no_version rather than linked to V1–V7. The paper also discusses earlier LLM findings; those cited results are not rows. Signature reproduction results are omitted because signatures are not the harmful-content behaviour at issue.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes concept-erased text-to-image diffusion models (ESD/SDD Stable Diffusion v1.4, FLUX.1) on benign anime datasets and measures unsafe image generation. The claim versions concern safety-trained language or chat models complying with harmful user requests, refusal, and token-position effects. Diffusion image generation is a different kind of system and outcome, so no row bears on V1–V7. The paper cites Qi et al. and draws the analogy explicitly but runs no LLM experiment. The analogous finding is recorded under fits_no_version. The record's 'tests/T3' with every version marked not_tested is inconsistent, so it is reset to discusses/T6.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that benign fine-tuning can undo safety alignment in text-to-image diffusion models, so suppressed concepts reappear and are even amplified. They attribute this to the fine-tuning LoRA learning the inverse of the safety LoRA. They propose Modular LoRA, which trains the task LoRA with the safety LoRA detached and merges them at inference, and call it an intermediate solution.
record.recipe_differences: Rather than fine-tuning aligned chat models and measuring refusal, this paper fine-tunes concept-erased diffusion models on benign image datasets and evaluates generated images. It also tests a modular LoRA mitigation.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome varies with the fine-tuning dataset, the full-versus-LoRA-versus-Modular method, prompt set, safety-removal method (ESD or SDD), training-set size and training stage. The appendix states that changing the fine-tuning learning rate changes the speed of jailbreaking.

fits_no_version.finding: Benign anime-dataset fine-tuning of ESD/SDD-erased SD v1.4 raises exposed-body-part rates. For example, ESD Full goes from 11.5% to 40.0% on Danbooru, and SDD LoRA from 3.7% to 38.5%. Q16 inappropriate rates rise for ESD, from 46.9% to 72.6%. The effect is stronger for datasets closer to the erased concept and appears early in training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benign fine-tuning reverses concept-erasure safety alignment in text-to-image diffusion models.

fits_no_version.finding: Training the task LoRA with the safety LoRA detached, then reattaching it, keeps unsafe rates low: 6.1% average for ESD and 1.8% for SDD on exposed body parts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Modular separation of safety and task adapters mitigates fine-tuning jailbreaks in diffusion models.

record.problems: The paper notes that NudeNet and Q16 can misclassify images and that small differences should not be treated as significant; manually reviewing all images was infeasible. It reports no uncertainty estimates. Several key image-generation outcomes are qualitative or figure-based. The flattened text for Table 3 does not securely map several SDD values to dataset columns.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 and Table 3 aggregate values were retained where their column assignments were clear; SDD values in Table 3 were not assigned to individual datasets because the flattened text does not establish the mapping. The more granular prompt-by-prompt results in Tables 7 and 8, additional figure-only curves and many qualitative image examples in Figures 5–12 and 14–16 were not separately extracted, to stay within the row limit and avoid duplicating outcomes already represented by the main tables. Table 4 artist-style similarity and Table 5 quality metrics were omitted because they do not measure unsafe-content behaviour. Signature-reproduction results were omitted because signatures are not the harmful-content measure at issue.

untested.parts: No harmful-data fine-tuning of chat/LLM models; only benign data is used, on diffusion models.
Benign fine-tuning raises unsafe image generation in diffusion models, but harmful-request compliance by language models is not measured.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks.
Safety is implemented as a LoRA by design; LoRA negation is shown in diffusion only, not for LLM safety localization.
Offers a diffusion-specific explanation (FT LoRA learns the inverse of the safety LoRA), not why LLM alignment is shallow.
Modular LoRA is a diffusion mitigation, not training that deepens safety beyond the first tokens.

record.verdict_notes: This is a cross-modal analogue of Qi et al. (V2-like) in diffusion models. It was kept out of the version links because the versions concern language-model harmful-request compliance. If the phenomenon file broadens V2 to generative models generally, the Table 2 and Table 1 rows would be observed for V2, except Full→LoRA on Table 1, which is absent or negligible. The Q16 SDD rows labelled Table 3 do not exist in Table 3 and should be deleted. The authors warn that NudeNet and Q16 have high false-positive rates and that small differences are not significant; no uncertainty estimates are given.

versions.untested_parts: Tests image generation after fine-tuning diffusion models, not harmful-request compliance or refusal by chat models.
Uses benign image datasets, but measures unsafe image generation rather than harmful-request compliance by chat models.
No compliant opening, adversarial suffix, or decoding-change test on chat models.
LoRA modules are used, but the study does not test whether a small set of parameters carries chat-model safety behaviour.
Offers an explanation for re-emergence in diffusion models; does not test why chat-model safety is shallow.
Modular LoRA is tested for diffusion-image safety, not training that spreads chat-model safety beyond initial response tokens.

rows.note: The authors state that this fine-tuning both relearns and amplifies the harmful concept.
rows.check: The 62% is W0+ΔWft with no safety LoRA attached. The relevant baselines in Fig. 13 are W0 alone (73%) and W0+ΔWft⋆ (32%). With safety attached, ΔWft gives 2% and ΔWft⋆ gives 1%. The baseline should be stated, and the subject is SD v1.4 (W0).

rows.subject: Dreambooth model; base model not stated
rows.operation_detail: Dreambooth fine-tuning using five sneaker images with the modular fine-tuning component
rows.measure: Percentage of generated images described as harmful
rows.note: The authors compare this with the standard fine-tuning result.
rows.check: Compares the study's own ΔWft⋆ with ΔWft, both without the safety LoRA (32% vs 62%). This is a method comparison, not a rate of the behaviour arising.
